Character speed is how fast the dits and dahs are sent. Farnsworth keeps each character at full speed but adds extra space between characters, down to the effective speed, so you have time to recognize each one. Applies to words, groups and other multi-character content — single characters are unaffected.

Below %1$s WPM it\'s easy to start counting the dits and dahs instead of hearing each character as a single sound. Training at %2$s+ WPM builds instant, by-ear recognition, which is the whole point of the Koch method. resources.string: How to begin, what to expect, and why it sounds so fast
If you\'ve never copied a character in your life, this is the whole path. It takes about five minutes to get going, and you\'ll be recognizing your first two letters by sound in one sitting.

string-array.name: start_here_step_bodies
string-array.item: Not required, but Morse is a listening exercise and phone speakers flatten the rhythm.
It\'s the first tile, and it\'s the guided path. It decides what to teach you and when.
A character plays and answer choices appear. Pick the one you heard. Miss, and the answer is revealed and re-sent so your ear gets a second pass.
At 33 WPM you physically can\'t, and that\'s deliberate. Let each character land as one sound, like a syllable. Too fast? Widen the gaps, never slow the characters.
Short and daily beats long and occasional. Turn on the daily reminder in Settings and let the streak do the nagging.

resources.string: Feeling lost in the first few sessions is normal and expected. The Koch method starts you at a speed you can\'t decode consciously, because conscious decoding is a dead end that caps you at about 10 WPM. The discomfort is the method working.
There are two different speeds, and they are set independently.
How fast the dits and dahs inside a letter are sent.
33 WPM or above, from day one. Never lower.
How fast text arrives once the silence between characters is counted.
Whatever you can currently handle. 5 WPM is fine.

You are not expected to copy at 33 WPM. You are expected to learn at 33 WPM. A character at 33 WPM with two seconds of silence after it is correct, normal, and exactly how a beginner\'s session should look.

At 33 WPM a character arrives too fast to count, so the only thing your brain can do is take it as a single sound — which is the skill you\'re building. Drop below about 33 and counting becomes possible, your brain takes the shortcut, and you build a habit you\'ll later have to break. When it feels too fast, widen the gaps (Farnsworth spacing) or raise the Recognition target. Never lower the character speed.

Your character speed is currently %1$d WPM, which is slow enough to count dits at. Raise it to 33 in Settings before the counting habit forms, and leave the Farnsworth speed wherever you\'re comfortable.
How the app decides what\'s next
The Koch method: you start with two characters at full speed. When you can reliably recognize them, a third is added, then a fourth. The speed never drops; only the number of characters grows.

Time-to-recognize: every answer is timed from the moment the last tone ends. Right in 0.4 seconds is learned; right in 3 seconds means you\'re still decoding it consciously. That timing drives which character comes next, when a new one unlocks, and your weakest-first stats. If you need more time to answer, raise the Recognition target — don\'t slow the code down.

resources.string: Have a target beyond "learn Morse". The best one is a real contact, and it needs far less than the full alphabet: your own callsign, the question mark, your state, and a handful of exchange words. People who aim at a contact tend to get there; people who aim at finishing the alphabet often stall.

Open Settings › Characters & Lessons › Proficiency and tell it what you already know. That sets your starting character set instead of making you re-earn A and N. Comfortable with the whole alphabet? Skip Journey and go straight to Common Words, Rapid Fire, or Pileup Runner.
Today\'s word in Morse — your speed, up to %1$d WPM
Your device appears to be muted
The volume is at or near zero. Every play before you solve the word counts as a listen, so turn it up first, or play anyway.

Drops %1$d WPM for every %2$d listens and for every %3$d wrong guesses, down to %4$d. Locked once you guess. Sent straight at that speed, with no Farnsworth spacing, so it is quicker than the same number in a drill.
No dit-dah reference — your share text says so.

One five-letter word a day, the same for everyone. Every %1$d listens and every %2$d wrong guesses slow the code by %3$d WPM — no limit on either — and your share text reports the slowest speed you heard it at. Green is the right letter in the right place, amber is the right letter somewhere else.
The word everyone got on %1$s. Practice only: it doesn\'t count toward your streak, change that day\'s result, or share.
Practice only — not counted and not shared.
The last %1$d days. Catch up on one you missed, or replay one, as practice.
Every Daily Dit from the last %1$d days. Open a day you missed, or replay one you copied — as practice: it doesn\'t count toward your streak or change that day\'s result.
TTR = time from the end of the tone to your answer. Green means mastered (fast & accurate); the slowest/weakest characters are listed first.
Characters you\'ve mixed up most often. Drill them head-to-head in the Confusion Drill mode — each one you get right eases the pair.

Keep Bluetooth audio awake plays a floor deliberately just above silence — too quiet to hear — so Bluetooth earbuds never idle between transmissions: truly silent audio lets some headsets sleep, and they wake a moment late and clip the first character.

Band noise adds audible band noise (QRN) while a mode, game or lesson is playing, so practicing is more like copying off the air; it stays quiet on the menus, and picking a level plays a short sample. Any level also keeps Bluetooth audio awake.

On-air etiquette for hunting Parks on the Air activators, one rule at a time.
New to CW on the air? Start with First Four
Your call, your state, ?, 73 — heard and sent

Procedure after WB0RLJ\'s “Advice for CW POTA Hunters”, with thanks, and the Parks on the Air CW Guide.
Jim Vaughan (WB0RLJ) on YouTube — his daily activations
\?, AGN?, AS, BK, SRI, QRZ?, dit-dit
No DE, no K, no repeats
Answer only if it\'s in your call
Who did they come back to?
Send an error, then send it again
Zero beat, RIT, XIT and the pileup
Say again — they didn\'t get it all
Dit-dit: the friendly sign-off. This contact is done.
Activators keep it short. These are the signals you\'ll hear most while hunting, and what each one asks of you.
An activator ends each contact with 73 or TU and two quick dits (E E). That dit-dit is your moment: call right away.
Don\'t wait for a CQ. In a pileup many activators never send one between contacts — the dit-dit is the invitation.
While a contact is going on — the activator is sending someone else\'s call, a report, or <AS> — stay quiet. Calling over it only slows everyone down.
The activator knows their own call, and you\'re on their frequency, so they already know who you\'re calling.
Send just your call, once. No DE, no K, no activator\'s call, no repeats. Then stop and listen.
Repeating your call doesn\'t get you through faster: it covers up the next round, and the activator may have been answering you.
When the activator sends part of a call and a ?, they\'re asking that station to send again.
Answer only if those characters are in your call — at the start, the middle or the end. If they aren\'t, it\'s someone else: stay quiet.
When it is yours, send your full call, once — never just the missing part. A bare ? means they heard someone and caught nothing: anyone who called can send again.
After you call, listen to who the activator comes back to. Your call: it\'s you — send your exchange.
Another call: that contact is in progress. Stay quiet until it ends with the dit-dit.
A call one letter from yours, like %1$s for %2$s, sent without a question mark: they\'re working %1$s. Stay silent.
The same call with a question mark (%1$s?): they\'re not sure what they heard. Send your call once, then listen for whether they come back with yours.
When they come back with your call, a report and their state, reply with your report, your state and 73: %1$s. That\'s the form First Four teaches.
WB0RLJ\'s order works too: report, state and BK (%1$s), then, after their TU 73 and dit-dit, %2$s. Either form is right here.
5NN is 599, the report nearly every POTA contact carries.
They finish with TU 73 and the dit-dit. Send E E (or 73 E E) back — then stop. The next QRZ? is for someone else.

Everyone fumbles a character. When you do, send an error, then send the word again, correctly, from the start: your whole call, not just the letter you fixed. Don\'t go quiet and hope; the activator may log what you sent.

An error isn\'t one fixed signal. It can be a quick run of dits, five to eight of them, or someone slapping the key: fast or slow, run together or ragged. Don\'t copy its shape. Recognise it, forget what came just before it, and copy what follows.
Here an error is shown as %1$s. Play the examples: no two sound alike.

Pitch. On CW, the tone you hear is how far the signal is from where your receiver is tuned, plus your rig\'s CW pitch setting. Your sidetone is set to that same pitch. So a station that sounds exactly like your sidetone is on the frequency you\'d transmit on.

Zero beat. Being on exactly the same frequency is called zero beat. Play two tones a few hertz apart and you hear a slow beat; at the same frequency the beat stops. Zero beat is how you get onto a station\'s frequency.

Offset. In a pileup, everyone zero beat sounds like one long tone and nobody gets copied. Call a little off — 20 to 100 Hz, the Parks on the Air CW Guide says — and you\'re on your own pitch in the activator\'s ears, still well inside their filter.

RIT, XIT and pitch. RIT moves what you hear and leaves where you transmit alone. XIT moves where you transmit and leaves what you hear alone. Pitch sets the tone you hear CW at, and your sidetone with it. A forgotten RIT is the classic way to call off frequency without meaning to.
Pitch (and the pitch line on the panadapter)
none built in: click-tune to the line
Models and firmware differ — check your manual.
What the activator hears when five hunters answer a CQ — one of them you, %1$s.
Five callers on one tone. Can you pick out %1$s?
The same pileup with you %1$d Hz up. Your call stands out.
Everyone on their own pitch. Now the activator can pick out each call.
The activator is calling %1$d Hz above you. Turn the RIT and listen: their pitch moves, but where you\'d transmit doesn\'t.
You hear them at %1$d Hz; your sidetone is %2$d Hz.
You\'d still call %1$d Hz from them.
The activator is somewhere off your frequency. Tune until they sound just like your sidetone — play them together and the beat slows and stops — then tap Done.
Zero beat — you\'re %1$d Hz from them.
Not yet: you\'re %1$d Hz above them. They were at %2$s Hz.
Not yet: you\'re %1$d Hz below them. They were at %2$s Hz.

Every one right. You\'re ready for the pileup.

You\'ve sent your exchange. The activator sends:
You\'ve sent E E back: the contact is done. Then you hear:
You meant to send your call, but keyed %1$s.
You keyed %1$s — only the last character is wrong.
A big pileup: everyone is calling exactly on the activator\'s frequency.
You want to hear the activator at your sidetone pitch without moving where you transmit.
You want to transmit 60 Hz off the activator without changing how they sound to you.
You need to retune your antenna tuner before you call.
1 kHz or more away, at low power
On their frequency, at low power
<AS> means wait. The activator will be back — don\'t call until they are.
QRZ? asks “who is calling me?” — an invitation to send your call.
Two quick dits are the friendly sign-off: that contact is done.
BK means back to you — it\'s your turn to send.
AGN? asks the station they\'re working to send it again.
That dit-dit ended their contact with %1$s. Call now — don\'t wait for a CQ.
They\'re sending %1$s a report: that contact is in progress. Stay quiet.
<AS> means wait. Calling now just adds noise; wait for them to come back.
Sorry, who\'s calling? That\'s an open invitation — send your call now.
Just your call, once. They know their own call, and DE and K add nothing.
QRZ? gets your call, once. Repeats cover up the next round.
Their contact is over: send your call, once — no need for theirs.
%1$s matches the start of your call. Send your full call, once.
%1$s isn\'t in your call — they want someone else. Stay quiet.
%1$s matches the end of your call. Send your full call, once.
They\'re missing one character, but send your whole call — a lone character means nothing on its own.
They came back to %1$s. Stay quiet until that contact ends.
That\'s you, with a report and their state. Send your exchange: %1$s, or %2$s in WB0RLJ\'s order.
No question mark: they\'re working %1$s, not you. Stay silent.
%1$s? is a question about a call close to yours. Send your call once, then listen for whether they come back with yours.
Report, state, 73 — or report, state, BK in WB0RLJ\'s order. Short and complete either way; save the ragchew for another time.
AGN? asks for your exchange again: send it again.
Send the dits back (E E, or 73 E E). That\'s the friendly close — and then you\'re done.
You\'re in the log. The next QRZ? is for someone else — stop and let them in.
Send an error, then your whole call, correctly. SRI isn\'t used for this.
After the error, send the whole call again — never just the fixed character.
An error, then resend from the word with the mistake: your state and 73.
That burst of dits — however many, however fast — was an error: forget %1$s and copy what follows. They have you, so send your exchange.
A small offset, 20–100 Hz, puts you on your own pitch and still inside their filter. 2 kHz up is off their frequency entirely.
RIT shifts what you hear without moving your transmit frequency.
XIT shifts where you transmit without moving what you hear.
Tune up 1 kHz or more away, at the lowest power that works — never on a busy frequency.
Arcade practice: every hit and miss feeds your stats, and each game has its own gentle speed ramp.

Characters fall from the top in columns. Hear one and type it, or see one and key it, to shoot the lowest invader carrying it before it reaches the ground. Three lives; every wave comes faster. Misses feed your confusion drill.
Tap an invader to hear it again

Sent from %1$d WPM, stepping up %2$d WPM after %3$d hits in a row (the first %4$d after any change do not count) to your %5$d WPM character speed. A landing steps it back %6$d WPM. Characters you miss come round more often until you master them.
Sent at your %1$d WPM character speed.
Decoded at your %1$d WPM character speed.

Enemies swoop in along curved paths and settle into a formation, then dive at you one by one. Hear one and type it, or see one and key it, to shoot the most dangerous enemy carrying it before its dive gets through. Consecutive hits build a combo multiplier up to ×8; three lives; every wave brings a bigger formation and faster dives. Misses feed your confusion drill.
Enemies fly in unmarked. Each one is sent in Morse as it enters and again as it dives (tap it to hear it again); type the character you heard to shoot the most dangerous one carrying it.
Each enemy shows its character. Key it on the on-screen key or a hardware key; the decoded character shoots the most dangerous one carrying it.
Sent from %1$d WPM, stepping up %2$d WPM every %3$d hits to your %4$d WPM character speed. A dive that gets through steps it back.
Tap an enemy to hear it again

Cities and ships line the bottom, each with a callsign. Attackers come down from the top, and each one sends the callsign of the asset it is heading for. Copy it and route the defense — tap that asset, or type the callsign — before the attacker arrives. Lose every asset and the game is over; every wave brings more assets and more attackers at once. Every copy feeds your character stats.
Four-character call-like groups spelled only from your active set: %1$s
Real US-style callsigns such as K1AB, AB1C, K1ABC and AB1CD.
Tap an attacker to hear it again · tap the asset it named
Tap an attacker to hear it again
Callsigns sent from %1$d WPM, stepping up %2$d WPM every %3$d hits to your %4$d WPM character speed. A lost asset steps it back.
Callsigns sent at your %1$d WPM character speed.
Farnsworth spacing at %1$d WPM effective applies.

A roguelike, room by room. Each monster casts a spell word in Morse; copy it, then key the counter word from the spell book on a Morse key before the attack lands. A counter in time hurts the monster, a wrong or late one costs a life, and some counters heal you. Three lives; every room\'s window is shorter. Every keyed character feeds your stats and confusion drill.
Hear the spell, key the counter. ♥ marks a counter that also heals you.
Your active characters spell fewer than %1$d pairs, so the starter spells are in use. They need the first ten Koch characters.
Spells are sent from %1$d WPM, stepping up %2$d WPM every %3$d counters to your %4$d WPM character speed. A hit taken steps it back.
Spells are sent at your %1$d WPM character speed.
Farnsworth spacing at %1$d WPM applies to the spell.
Tap a monster to hear its spell again

Hop a frog across three lanes of traffic and three of river. Every vehicle and log carries a character, and each lane is cued in Morse: only the cued vehicle is harmless and only the cued log floats. Three lives; each crossing is a wave and the traffic gets faster. Labels hide as the waves go on. Wrong lanes feed your confusion drill.
Tap the board to hear the next lane\'s cue again
Labels hide three seconds after the cue: keep your eye on the one you heard. Tap the board to hear the cue again
Tap the board to hear the next lane\'s cue again; the traffic announces itself
Cues sent from %1$d WPM, stepping up %2$d WPM every %3$d safe crossings of a lane to your %4$d WPM character speed. Losing a life steps it back.
Cues sent at your %1$d WPM character speed.

Labels show for the first two crossings. From the third, a lane\'s labels show for three seconds after its cue and then hide, so keep your eye on the one you heard. From the fifth, the traffic announces itself in Morse instead.
Wave %1$d: labels hide after the cue
Wave %1$d: no labels, listen to the traffic

Labeled asteroids drift in toward your ship. See one and key its label to destroy it, or hear one sent and tap the asteroid carrying it. Later waves bring short words and callsigns that split into their characters when hit. Three lives; every wave comes faster. Misses feed your confusion drill.
From wave %1$d, larger asteroids carry short words and callsigns spelled from these characters; a word splits into its characters when hit.
Sent from %1$d WPM, stepping up %2$d WPM every %3$d hits to your %4$d WPM character speed. An asteroid that reaches the ship steps it back.

Hunting a Parks on the Air activator takes four things: your callsign, your state, ? and 73. First Four teaches you to hear and send each one, then walks you through the contact itself.

Find an activator on a spotting page, listen until you have their call, and call them.

A first CW contact is a big deal — for you, and often for the activator too. Afterwards, consider following up: send a QSL card, drop them an email, or just a thank-you note. Many activators love hearing they were someone\'s first.
Your call is the one thing you send in every contact — and the thing you most need to hear when it comes back to you.
Hunters send their state as their part of a POTA exchange.
\? (di-di-dah-dah-di-dit) means “say again.” An activator sends it when they only caught part of a call.
73 means best regards. It is how a contact ends.
%1$d right in a row to move on to sending.
%1$d right in a row to pass this stage.

Activators often catch only part of a call. When they send a piece of yours with a ?, send your full call again — then stop and wait for them to come back to you.
Calling and hearing nothing back is normal: the activator may not hear you, or may be answering someone else. Here is what to do in each case.
A whole minimal POTA contact from the hunter\'s side: they call CQ, you call them, they send your report and their state, you send yours and 73.

resources.string: Not quite. Replay it and listen for the state after 5NN.
Stay quiet: they\'re working another station. Calling over a contact only makes it harder for everyone. Tap Wait.
%1$s is calling CQ POTA — asking any station to answer.
Your turn: send your call, once. Then stop and listen.
Just “?”: they heard someone calling, but not who. Send your call again.
“%1$s”: they caught part of a call. It matches yours, so they want you to send it again.
Send your full call — then wait for them to come back to you.
Your call, 5NN and their state: they\'ve got you. From here the contact goes on as usual.
Nothing came back. That\'s normal — they may not have heard you, or heard several stations at once.
Call again: send your call once more, then listen.
They came back to another hunter. That contact is now in progress.
Don\'t send while they work the other station. Wait and listen.
TU 73 ends that contact, and QRZ asks “who is calling?” Your turn to call again.
They sent your call, 5NN (the signal report, 599) and their state, twice. Type their state.
Send your exchange: 5NN, your state, and 73.
TU 73 and two dits: you\'re in the log. That is a complete contact!
